metadata.title: Effects of Teacher Collaboration on Teaching Practices in China and England: A Structural Equation Model With TALIS 2018 Data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for China and England, applying TALIS’s two-stage sampling design (schools sampled within region/teacher-count strata, then teachers sampled within schools). The manuscript describes the sampling procedure but does not report the use of TALIS sampling weights or any specific weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) in the SEM estimation. Because the analysis is based on Mplus maximum likelihood estimation with robust standard errors and bootstrap mediation, the paper does not document whether complex-survey weighting was incorporated into the SEM/bootstrapping steps. The analytic sample is restricted to lower-secondary teachers in the two countries (and, for China, drawn from Shanghai), but the paper does not specify additional exclusions such as missing-item handling rules.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study models latent constructs from TALIS questionnaire items (teacher collaboration, teacher self-efficacy, and teaching practices) using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling; these are not cognitive achievement scores with plausible values. The paper also does not report a missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise/pairwise deletion or multiple imputation) for the SEM/bootstrapped mediation, which is a reporting gap because missingness can affect parameter estimates and indirect effects.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 teacher data for China and England. The paper restricts the Chinese sample to Shanghai (not representative of all Chinese regions) and limits the analysis to lower-secondary teachers. TALIS’s two-stage sampling is described (schools sampled within strata; then 20 teachers sampled per school, or all qualified teachers if fewer than 20). Beyond these restrictions, the manuscript does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., handling of missing questionnaire items) for the final analytic sample.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (teachers), China (Shanghai) and England (lower-secondary), teaching practices: clarity of instruction (CLAIN)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM standardized paths (China): COLES→CLAIN b=2.006 (p>.05, not significant); EXCH→CLAIN b=.206 (p<.01); SELF→CLAIN b=.399 (p<.001). SEM standardized paths (England): COLES→CLAIN b=.044 (p>.05, not significant); EXCH→CLAIN b=.118 (p<.05); SELF→CLAIN b=.553 (p<.001). Mediation (indirect via SELF): China COLES→CLAIN b=.109 (p=.000, 95% CI [0.064, 0.161]); EXCH→CLAIN no indirect effect. England COLES→CLAIN b=.132 (p=.000, 95% CI [0.071, 0.193]).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher data from China (Shanghai) and England (lower-secondary), the study leveraged exchange and co-ordination, professional collaboration, and teacher self-efficacy to model clarity of instruction (CLAIN), finding that exchange and co-ordination had a positive direct association with clarity of instruction in both countries while professional collaboration was not significantly related to clarity of instruction. The study also found that professional collaboration showed significant indirect effects on clarity of instruction via teacher self-efficacy (in both China and England), indicating that strengthening teacher self-efficacy may help translate professional collaboration into clearer instructional practices, even though direct effects of professional collaboration on clarity may be weak or absent. main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (teachers), China (Shanghai) and England (lower-secondary), teaching practices: cognitive activation (COGAC)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM standardized paths (China): COLES→COGAC b=.080 (p>.05, not significant); EXCH→COGAC b=.067 (p>.05, not significant); SELF→COGAC b=.341 (p<.001). SEM standardized paths (England): COLES→COGAC b=.406 (p<.001); EXCH→COGAC b=−2.173 (p<.01); SELF→COGAC b=.437 (p<.001). Mediation (indirect via SELF): China COLES→COGAC b=.093 (p=.000, 95% CI [0.053, 0.138]); EXCH→COGAC no indirect effect. England COLES→COGAC b=.104 (p=.000, 95% CI [0.058, 0.145]).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher data from China (Shanghai) and England (lower-secondary), the study leveraged exchange and co-ordination, professional collaboration, and teacher self-efficacy to model cognitive activation (COGAC), finding that professional collaboration was not significantly related to cognitive activation in China but was positively associated with cognitive activation in England. The study also found that exchange and co-ordination was not significant in China yet showed a negative direct association with cognitive activation in England, while teacher self-efficacy was positively associated with cognitive activation in both countries. Finally, professional collaboration had significant indirect effects on cognitive activation via teacher self-efficacy in both countries, indicating that policies aiming to raise teachers’ self-efficacy may be a key mechanism through which professional collaboration supports higher-order, cognitively activating instruction, though the effect of lower-level exchange/co-ordination may differ by context. main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (teachers), China (Shanghai) and England (lower-secondary), teaching practices: classroom assessment (ASS)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM standardized paths (China): COLES→ASS b=.020 (p>.05, not significant); EXCH→ASS b=.261 (p<.01); SELF→ASS b=.426 (p<.001). SEM standardized paths (England): COLES→ASS b=.152 (p<.05); EXCH→ASS b=.073 (p>.05, not significant); SELF→ASS b=.325 (p<.001). Mediation (indirect via SELF): China COLES→ASS b=.166 (p=.000, 95% CI [0.068, 0.173]); EXCH→ASS no indirect effect. England COLES→ASS b=.078 (p=.000, 95% CI [0.042, 0.114]).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher data from China (Shanghai) and England (lower-secondary), the study leveraged exchange and co-ordination, professional collaboration, and teacher self-efficacy to model classroom assessment (ASS), finding that exchange and co-ordination had a positive direct association with classroom assessment in China but not in England, while professional collaboration was not significant for classroom assessment in China yet was positively associated in England. Teacher self-efficacy showed a positive direct association with classroom assessment in both countries. The study further found significant indirect effects of professional collaboration on classroom assessment via teacher self-efficacy in both China and England, indicating that improving teacher self-efficacy may help professional collaboration translate into more frequent classroom assessment practices, even when direct effects vary across national contexts. data.outcome_summary: This study uses TALIS 2018 teacher survey data for China (Shanghai) and England, focusing on lower-secondary teachers and modeling three teaching-practice latent constructs: clarity of instruction (CLAIN), cognitive activation (COGAC), and classroom assessment (ASS). The authors estimate confirmatory factor models and a structural equation model using maximum likelihood with robust standard errors in Mplus 7.4, and test mediation via bootstrap confidence intervals (Hayes, 2009). Across both countries, teacher self-efficacy is positively associated with all three teaching-practice subscales (e.g., SELF→CLAIN b=.399 in China; b=.553 in England). Professional collaboration shows significant indirect effects on all three teaching practices through self-efficacy in both countries (e.g., COLES→COGAC via SELF: b=.093 in China; b=.104 in England), while exchange/co-ordination has more mixed direct and no indirect mediation effects. Limitations include the absence of reported missing-data handling and unclear use of TALIS complex-survey weights, so results should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.
